content: Lesser celandine, scientifically known as Ranunculus ficaria (synonyms include Ficaria grandiflora Robert and Ficaria verna Huds.), is a low-growing, hairless perennial plant characterized by its fleshy, dark green, heart-shaped leaves. According to the diarist Gilbert White, who wrote in the Hampshire village of Selborne around 1800, the plant typically emerged on February 21st. However, it is more commonly observed to flower from March to May, earning it the nickname spring messenger. The flowers are yellow when they bloom but gradually turn white as they age. This species exists in two chromosomal forms: diploid (2n = 16) and tetraploid (2n = 32). While both forms are visually similar, the tetraploid variant tends to prefer shadier environments and often develops bulbils at the base of its stalk. These two forms are sometimes classified as distinct subspecies, referred to as R. ficaria ficaria and R. ficaria bulbifer, respectively. Lesser celandine is native to Europe and western Asia but has been introduced to North America. It thrives in bare, damp soil and is often considered a persistent garden weed in the United Kingdom. Historically, the plant was known as pilewort due to its use in treating hemorrhoids. This association arose from the resemblance of its knobby tubers to piles, a connection rooted in the Doctrine of Signatures, which suggested that the physical appearance of a plant indicated its medicinal uses. In German, the plant is called Scharbockskraut (scurvywort), a name derived from the early leaves' high vitamin C content, which was used to combat scurvy. The poet William Wordsworth was particularly fond of the flower, which inspired him to write three poems, including an ode to the celandine. Upon Wordsworth's death, it was proposed that a celandine be carved on his memorial plaque inside the church of Saint Oswald in Grasmere. Unfortunately, the Greater celandine (Chelidonium majus) was mistakenly used instead. In many regions of the northern United States and Canada, lesser celandine is classified as an invasive species.
